items.text: Late diagnosis doesn't just bring relief. It brings grief — for the years of self-blame that turned out to have a different explanation. Both things arrive at once. Nobody warns you that's normal.
items.rationale: Names the duality the briefing identifies as underserved — relief and grief coexisting — without explaining it away. The final beat ('nobody warns you that's normal') delivers the recognition hit that makes validation posts shareable.

items.text: Having a name for what you've experienced doesn't erase the years before it. It means rewriting the story you told yourself about why you struggled — and that's its own kind of work.
items.rationale: Second take on late-diagnosis grief from a different entry point: the active labour of identity reconstruction rather than the simultaneous emotional experience. Pairs with post 1 without repeating it.

items.text: Autistic burnout isn't weakness. It's what happens when a nervous system has been running an overdraft for years. The body eventually closes the account.
items.rationale: The financial metaphor ('overdraft', 'closes the account') is concrete and shame-free without claiming clinical precision. Delivers the reframe in three short beats that build to a hard stop.
items.sensitivity_flag: Nervous-system 'overdraft' is a metaphor — verify it reads as evocative analogy and not a clinical explanation of physiological mechanism.

items.text: 'I thought I was just lazy.' That sentence shows up in almost every burnout story. It wasn't laziness. It was a nervous system trying to survive conditions it was never built for.
items.rationale: Opens with a quoted self-talk phrase for instant recognition, then reframes without lecturing. 'Almost every burnout story' avoids universalising while still conveying this experience is widespread.

items.text: AuDHD isn't a quirky abbreviation. It's what people reached for when every existing clinical category described them halfway and left the rest unexplained.
items.rationale: Treats the community-coined term with the seriousness it's earned. The 2026 SAGE study makes this defensible — peer-reviewed research is now studying the gap the word was coined to fill.

items.text: 'Half-right everywhere' is how a lot of AuDHD people describe life before that word existed. Not fully wrong. Not fully fitting. Just never quite the whole shape of any category.
items.rationale: Names a specific felt experience rather than explaining a diagnosis. 'A lot of' rather than 'all' keeps it accurate. The phrase 'whole shape' is distinctive and quotable without being clinical.

items.text: Declarative language isn't a script you run. It's what naturally comes out when you've stopped trying to manage someone and started trying to understand them.
items.rationale: Captures the briefing's core nuance — it's a relational stance, not a technique — in two sentences. Generous to parents and educators who found it 'didn't work' without blaming them for that.

items.text: 70% of neurodivergent employees don't feel safe disclosing at work. What would actually have to change — not in theory, in your actual workplace — for that number to move?
items.rationale: The stat earns the question; 'not in theory, in your actual workplace' pushes past abstract answers to genuine discussion. Avoids naming or dunking on employers. Opens debate without prescribing an answer.
items.sensitivity_flag: Stat is from a single Forbes survey (self-report); post should not upgrade it beyond what the source supports. Current framing ('don't feel safe') maps cleanly to the source's 'fear disclosure' finding.

items.text: Low-demand parenting isn't the absence of structure. It's the absence of adversarial structure. Those are two very different things.
items.rationale: The shortest post in the set — lean by design. The contrast lands harder for being compressed. Directly addresses the misreading that causes PDA families to stall, without blaming them for it.

items.text: 'Demand avoidance' asks how to stop it. 'Drive for autonomy' asks how to honour it. What you call something shapes every response that follows.
items.rationale: Three-beat structure: old frame, new frame, the principle that connects them. Mirrors the identity-first language debate this audience already cares about, making the analogy immediately legible.

items.text: ADHD doesn't make you unreliable. It creates a consistent gap between intention and follow-through that shame doesn't close — but different scaffolding can.
items.rationale: Moves from moral framing ('unreliable') to structural framing ('scaffolding') in a single sentence. 'Shame doesn't close' names the approach people have already tried and failed with. Evergreen enough to stand without a specific source.

items.text: If you keep setting intentions you can't follow through on, the problem probably isn't willpower. External structure — a timer, a specific place, a body double — does the work the ADHD brain can't generate alone.
items.rationale: Concrete and actionable; names three low-barrier strategies without prescribing a regimen. 'Probably' keeps it honest. 'The ADHD brain' is established community shorthand, not a diagnostic claim.
